replacement: The foundation of this town was evidently meant to annoy Euboea, since the passage across to Cenaeum in that island is a short one. At first it caused some alarm at Athens, which the event, however, did nothing to justify, for the town never gave the Athenians any trouble. The reason was as follows. The Thessalians were sovereign in those parts, and their territory was menaced by the foundation of the town. They were afraid that it might prove a very powerful neighbor, and so they continually harassed and made war on the new settlers, until they wore them out, in spite of their originally considerable numbers, since people flocked from all quarters to a place founded by the Lacedaemonians and therefore thought secure of prosperity. On the other hand, the Lacedaemonians themselves, in the persons of their governors, did their full share toward ruining its prosperity and reducing its population. They frightened away the greater part of the inhabitants by governing harshly and in some cases unfairly, and so made it easier for their neighbors to prevail against them.

note: "might be surrounded" strengthened to "would be surrounded".
replacement: At daybreak the two forces united, sat down at the place called Metropolis and encamped. Not long after, the Athenians in the twenty ships entered the Ambracian Gulf to support the Argives, bringing Demosthenes, two hundred Messenian heavy infantry and sixty Athenian archers. While the fleet off Olpae blockaded the hill from the sea, the Acarnanians and a few Amphilochians had already reached Argos. Most of the Amphilochians were held back by force by the Ambraciots. They were making ready to give battle to the enemy, and had chosen Demosthenes to command the whole allied army along with their own generals. Demosthenes led them near Olpae and encamped, a great ravine lying between the two armies. For five days they stayed inactive, and on the sixth both sides drew up in order of battle. The Peloponnesian army was the larger and outflanked its opponents. Demosthenes feared that his right might be surrounded. In a sunken road overgrown with bushes he therefore hid some four hundred heavy infantry and light troops. At the moment of the onset they were to rise behind the enemy’s projecting left wing and attack it in the rear. When both sides were ready, they joined battle. Demosthenes stood on the right wing with the Messenians and a few Athenians. The rest of the line consisted of the different divisions of the Acarnanians and the Amphilochian carters. The Peloponnesians and Ambraciots were drawn up all mixed together, except for the Mantineans, who were massed on the left, though they did not reach the end of the wing. There Eurylochus and his men faced the Messenians and Demosthenes.
